content: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Mon, 26 Oct 2026 20:13:12 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.11 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Crunchbase Data Shows Q3 Robotics Startup Funding Jumps 185% As US And China Lead Physical AI Push https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/q3-2026-us-china-robotics-startup-funding-jumps-physical-ai-push/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 11:00:53 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94284 Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with the bulk of investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data 1 . It was the latest in a run of quarters with nearly $10 billion or more in funding. Funding to the robotics sector in Q1 through Q3 2026 is up around 185% year over year. China and the US lead The bulk of robotics funding this year has been in China, with $13.2 billion invested, and the U.S., with $12.1 billion. Germany, the third-largest recipient of robotics startup funding, trails with $1.7 billion invested. The largest rounds in China went to Guangzhou-based Xpeng Robotics , a builder of AI models and physical robots that raised $900 million, and Shenzhen’s AI² Robotics , which is working to build intelligent robots for manufacturing, healthcare and services and raised a $736 million Series C round. In the U.S., billion-dollar rounds have also been raised this year by companies including Travis Kalanick ’s Los Angeles-based Atoms — which includes its ghost kitchen business, and divisions for robotics in mining and transport — and Pittsburgh-based Skild AI , which raised $1.4 billion for its robotics foundation model Skild Brain. Another notable round this year went to Germany-based Neura Robotics , which raised $1.4 billion for its cognitive robots, with AI and data infrastructure to build intelligence. Building out the data and model layer “We’re just seeing physical AI take off,” Ulrik Stig Hansen , co-CEO of San Francisco-based Encord , a provider of the data layer for physical AI, told Crunchbase News at its inaugural Long Horizon Physical AI Summit in San Francisco earlier this month. The compute and storage capabilities are being developed to support these systems, he noted, but building for the physical world takes time, especially compared to large language models trained on the vast troves of text on the internet. “Physical AI is very different because there is no internet of physical AI data, and so the data first has to be collected, and you have to convert it from sensor tokens to action tokens,” he said. Data sets are orders of magnitude larger for physical AI, requiring multimodal data combining vision, tactile, force and torque. “Storing all that data, curating all that data, enriching all that data, and validating that all the data works for these systems is a very expensive operation,” said Hansen. We are still in the pre-training phase of physical AI, but will soon be entering the post-training phase, he noted. More winners Around 75 robotics companies on the unicorn board have raised funding in the past three years. Of these, more than half — 45 — joined the board just this year. Among the most highly valued robotics startups, many competing companies are building data and models, as well as varied vertical use cases in heavy industry, manufacturing, logistics and household and use cases among others. Robotics funding is surging and new unicorns are emerging, but the sector’s direction remains uncertain as companies race toward further breakthroughs over the next year. “There are a lot of companies that are raising capital, and I think a lot of them are going to win, just because there’s so many different types of applications to the physical world,” said Hansen. Miss it in bad faith, and the penalty can reach twice the deposit. That deadline doesn’t care whether the letter was supposed to come from a person or a piece of software. Either way, someone will answer for it. I think about this a lot. At my company, Get Covered , we now run 16 AI agents across more than 3 million rental units. When we built them, the technical questions turned out to be the easier ones. The harder question, for each agent, was actually who it reports to. Rick Folgmann, COO at Get Covered. Most companies are about to face that same question, and few are ready for it. Deloitte’s 2026 State of AI survey found that 23% of companies use agentic AI at least moderately today, and 74% expect to within two years. Gartner , meanwhile, has predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. Those numbers make a case for running agents the way you would run staff in a regulated job, with written rules, a defined scope, a manager and a regular review. Here is what has worked for us, and what I would advise any decision-maker to focus on when it comes to scaling. Start with work that already has a rulebook The best early candidates for agents are tasks where the rules already exist somewhere outside anyone’s head: a statute, a contract clause, an insurance requirement in a vendor agreement. Take vendor certificates of insurance. Across the industry, property teams spend roughly three hours per property every week chasing those documents by email. The work is tedious, however at the same time, it is completely specified. Assignments like these give decision-makers two advantages. First, the agent has something objective to check its output against, and second, your team can audit the result without debating judgment calls. McKinsey ‘s most recent State of AI research found that the small group of companies seeing significant bottom-line returns from AI, about 6% of respondents, were nearly 3x as likely to have fundamentally redesigned their workflows. In my experience, that redesign starts with writing the rule down. If a new hire couldn’t follow your description of a decision on the person’s first day, an agent won’t follow it either. Set autonomy by workflow Tech execs I speak with often ask whether an AI system is autonomous, as if that were a fixed property of the product. In practice, the same agent should run with different levels of freedom depending on what it touches. At Get Covered, we configure each agent on different levels. For instance, a reminder to a vendor whose certificate expires next month can go out automatically. A response to a resident who has requested an emotional support animal never does. A useful exercise for any leadership team is to list every workflow an agent will touch and ask one question about each: If this action is wrong, how long until we find out, and what will it have cost by then?
